newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. Security Council to meet on Mideast crisis.
newsitem.headline: U.N. Security Council to meet on Mideast crisis.

text.p: By Nicholas Doughty, Diplomatic Correspondent
The U.N. Security Council, urged on by Arab states, agreed on Thursday to hold a formal debate on the Israeli-Palestinian crisis as fears grew that the Middle East peace process is about to collapse.

The 15-nation Security Council met for private consultations on Thursday and agreed, despite U.S. reluctance, to convene a formal meeting on Friday at 1100 EDT (1500 GMT). Foreign ministers from some countries are expected to attend.

More than 50 people, mostly Palestinians, have been killed in clashes in Gaza and the West Bank, leading to widespread Arab and European criticism of Israel's right-wing government and accusations that it is reneging on peace.

Council President Alfredo Lopes Cabral of Guinea-Bissau announced the meeting, to which the United States -- Israel's chief ally -- agreed only reluctantly, saying there was little point in "rhetorical debate" when practical steps were needed.
The Palestinian Authority, Saudi Arabia and Egypt had all requested a formal meeting of the Security Council. Egypt is the only current Arab member of the council.
Egypt's U.N. ambassador, Nabil Elaraby, told reporters Arab nations would draft a resolution for Friday's meeting. "The situation is quite explosive," he said.

Arab sources said the resolution would seek the closing of an Israeli-excavated archaeological tunnel in the Old City of Jerusalem, near Islamic and Jewish holy places, which sparked Palestinian protest demonstrations.

The group also wants the council to demand that Israel resume the Middle East peace process and abide by agreements already concluded with the Palestinian Authority by Israel's previous Labour government.
"We are not hoping for debate only, but for action," said Nasser al-Kidwa, the Palestinians' U.N. observer.
The chances of Friday's council meeting endorsing strong criticism of Israel are slim, since the United States has the power to block any condemnation with its veto.
In Washington, President Bill Clinton urged Israelis and Palestinians to end the bloodshed as his top officials engaged in frantic diplomatic efforts to salvage the peace process.
Clinton made clear that the U.S. government saw Israel's opening of a tourist tunnel near Moslem holy sites in east Jerusalem as an irritant.
Secretary of State Warren Christopher, in a telephone conversation with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu asked that the tunnel be closed, diplomatic sources said.
But Netanyahu responded that shutting the tunnel down was not a viable political option and argued such action would be seen as rewarding violence, the sources said.

Islamic and European nations, gathered in New York for the annual U.N. General Assembly, warned on Thursday that the crisis posed a grave threat to the whole peace process and criticised Israel, saying Netanyahu's Likud government would have to show it was committed to peace.
Arab anger at Netanyahu's failure to extend self-rule in the West Bank and Gaza boiled over after his government opened the tunnel near the al-Aqsa and Dome of the Rock mosques.
British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind said there was danger the peace process could be on the verge of collapse.
U.N. Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali appealed for calm and said previous peace agreements should be implemented.

Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring, who speaks for the 15-nation European Union as his country currently holds the EU presidency, said he had conveyed to Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy "our deepest concern".

"We emphasised very strongly and affirmatively the concern of the European Union that it was necessary for Israel to show ... a renewed commitment to the process. ... Signals need to be given by the Israeli government," he said.

Islamic nations also met to discuss the crisis and issued a statement afterwards criticising Israel, calling on it to honour previous agreements and condemning the opening of the tunnel as "an illegal act".
